problems.e: 8192 maps to 16384 (3 B); 1 maps to 2 (1 B); -30 maps to 59 (1 B); -1 maps to 1 (1 B), for 6 bytes. Without zigzag, a negative number in two's complement would look huge and take the maximum number of bytes.

problems.q: Signed coordinate deltas are written with zigzag encoding, which maps n to 2n when n is at least 0 and to -2n - 1 when n is negative, and the result is stored as a variable-length integer (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes do the deltas -100, 700, -8191, 64, -5 take?
problems.e: -100 maps to 199 (2 B); 700 maps to 1400 (2 B); -8191 maps to 16381 (2 B); 64 maps to 128 (2 B); -5 maps to 9 (1 B), for 9 bytes. Without zigzag, a negative number in two's complement would look huge and take the maximum number of bytes.

problems.q: Signed coordinate deltas are written with zigzag encoding, which maps n to 2n when n is at least 0 and to -2n - 1 when n is negative, and the result is stored as a variable-length integer (7 payload bits per byte). How many bytes do the deltas 8192, 700, 64, 1, 1, -1 take?
problems.e: 8192 maps to 16384 (3 B); 700 maps to 1400 (2 B); 64 maps to 128 (2 B); 1 maps to 2 (1 B); 1 maps to 2 (1 B); -1 maps to 1 (1 B), for 10 bytes. Without zigzag, a negative number in two's complement would look huge and take the maximum number of bytes.

label: Tcl evaluation and substitution
lesson:
# Tcl evaluation and substitution

Most EDA tools, OpenROAD and OpenSTA included, are driven by Tcl, and SDC constraint files are Tcl programs. Tcl's evaluation rules are short but unusual: everything is a string, a command is a list of words, and substitution happens once, before the command runs, in ways that braces and quotes control. Tool builders must know these rules to write command parsers, to read SDC correctly, and to avoid subtle scripting bugs such as integer division that differs from C.

## Words and lists

A Tcl command is a sequence of words separated by white space; the first word names the command. A Tcl list has the same syntax: elements separated by spaces, with braces grouping several words into one element. The command llength counts top-level elements. In the list u1 {a b c} u2 {} {x {y z}}, written inside outer braces, there are five elements: u1, the group a b c, u2, an empty element, and the group x {y z}. Nesting does not matter to llength; a braced group is one element however much it contains, and an empty pair of braces is a legal empty element. Tool commands that return collections of objects, such as the get commands of SDC, return lists or list-like handles, and scripts iterate them with foreach. A list built by string concatenation can split wrongly when names contain spaces, so scripts should build lists with the list command.

## Substitution in quotes and braces

Before a command runs, Tcl performs one round of substitution on each word: a dollar sign followed by a variable name is replaced by the variable's value, and a bracketed command such as [set w] is replaced by that command's result. Double quotes group a word but still allow substitution. Braces group a word and suppress all substitution. So after set w U42, the command set s "inst_[set w]/Z" stores inst_U42/Z, 10 characters, while set s {inst_[set w]/Z} stores the literal text inst_[set w]/Z, 14 characters. Substitution happens exactly once: if a value contains brackets, they are not evaluated again. This matters for EDA names, which often contain brackets for bus bits such as data[3]: a script must brace or escape them, or Tcl will try to run a command named 3.

## Integer arithmetic in expr

The expr command evaluates arithmetic. Its argument should be braced, as in expr {a + b} with variables, so that expr itself performs substitution once and can compile the expression; unbraced expressions are substituted twice and are slower and less safe. Integer division in Tcl rounds toward negative infinity, and the remainder takes the sign of the divisor, so that $a = b \cdot q + r$ always holds. Thus expr {17 / 5} is 3 and expr {17 % 5} is 2, but expr {-17 / 5} is -4 and expr {-17 % 5} is 3, and expr {17 % -5} is -3. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, giving -3 and -2 for the negative cases. A grid-snapping formula ported from C++ to a Tcl script can therefore snap negative coordinates differently. Mixing in a floating-point operand, as in 7 / 2.0, gives 3.5.

## Going deeper

John Ousterhout and Ken Jones, "Tcl and the Tk Toolkit" (2nd ed., 2009), the chapters on syntax and expressions; the Tcl manual page Tcl(n), which states the evaluation rules.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does the command `llength {{b core} {clk u2} {n12 b u2}}` return?
problems.e: llength counts top-level elements. A braced group, however much it contains and even when empty, is one element, so the list {{b core} {clk u2} {n12 b u2}} has 3 elements.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does the command `llength {{c rst met2} {u2 in0 y} {a core} {met2 {core clk}} clk}` return?
problems.e: llength counts top-level elements. A braced group, however much it contains and even when empty, is one element, so the list {{c rst met2} {u2 in0 y} {a core} {met2 {core clk}} clk} has 5 elements.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does the command `llength {{y c} core met1 u2 a u2}` return?
problems.e: llength counts top-level elements. A braced group, however much it contains and even when empty, is one element, so the list {{y c} core met1 u2 a u2} has 6 elements.

problems.q: A Tcl script runs `set w n1077` and then `set s "inst_[set w]/Z"`. Which value does `string length [set s]` return?
problems.e: Inside double quotes Tcl performs command substitution, so [set w] is replaced by n1077 and s becomes inst_n1077/Z, which has 12 characters.

problems.q: A Tcl script runs `set w n1077` and then `set s "[set w]"`. Which value does `string length [set s]` return?
problems.e: Inside double quotes Tcl performs command substitution, so [set w] is replaced by n1077 and s becomes n1077, which has 5 characters.

problems.q: A Tcl script runs `set w reg_a` and then `set s {top/[set w].A1}`. Which value does `string length [set s]` return?
problems.e: Inside braces Tcl performs no substitution, so s holds the literal text top/[set w].A1, which has 14 characters.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does `expr {10 / 6}` return?
problems.e: Tcl integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so 10 / 6 = 1, and the remainder 10 % 6 = 4 has the sign of the divisor, keeping a = b x quotient + remainder: 6 x 1 + 4 = 10. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, a classic porting bug.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does `expr {37 % 4}` return?
problems.e: Tcl integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so 37 / 4 = 9, and the remainder 37 % 4 = 1 has the sign of the divisor, keeping a = b x quotient + remainder: 4 x 9 + 1 = 37. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, a classic porting bug.

problems.q: In Tcl, which value does `expr {-33 / 7}` return?
problems.e: Tcl integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so -33 / 7 = -5, and the remainder -33 % 7 = 2 has the sign of the divisor, keeping a = b x quotient + remainder: 7 x -5 + 2 = -33. C and C++ truncate toward zero instead, a classic porting bug.

label: Tcl and Python tool APIs
lesson:
# Tcl and Python tool APIs

EDA engines are written in C++ for speed, but users and flows drive them from scripts. OpenROAD exposes its engines and its OpenDB database through a Tcl shell and through Python. The scripting layer is how flows are built, how reports are customized and, increasingly, how agents call tools. Designing that layer well decides what can be automated cheaply, what must be compiled, and how safe and reproducible scripted runs are.

## Scripting shells over compiled engines

In a modern EDA tool the command language is a thin layer. A global-placement command typed in the OpenROAD Tcl shell parses its options and calls into the C++ placer, which reads and edits the shared database; no placement arithmetic happens in Tcl. Tcl has stayed the industry's command language because it is small and easy to embed in a C or C++ program, and because SDC, the constraint language, is Tcl. Python is the second interface: OpenROAD can run with a Python interpreter and expose the database objects and engine calls, which suits data analysis and machine-learning experiments. The bindings are usually generated rather than handwritten: a wrapper generator such as SWIG reads interface descriptions of the C++ classes and emits glue code for each language, so one C++ API serves both.

## What to script and what to compile

Every call from a script into C++ crosses a boundary that costs far more than a simple getter. A Python loop that calls one location getter on each of 2,000,000 instances pays that overhead 2,000,000 times and can take minutes, while the same loop in C++ takes milliseconds. The rule follows: scripts orchestrate, configure and report; inner loops are compiled. A custom report of nets with more than 50 sinks and their drivers is a script over the database API. A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times is a compiled extension. Between the two sit bulk calls: a command that returns all locations at once, or that accepts a whole list of objects, moves the loop into C++ while keeping the script in control. Good APIs offer such bulk operations for the queries users run most.

## Designing a script API

Several rules separate a robust script API from a fragile one. Commands should accept and return object handles or collections rather than names, so a script does not convert 100,000 objects to strings and look each up again. Handles must be validated: if a script holds a handle to a net that another command deleted, the API should raise a script error rather than read freed memory. Configuration should travel as explicit command options or configuration objects, not as global variables whose last writer wins, so that each call is reproducible and loggable. C++ exceptions must be caught at the boundary and turned into script errors. When the caller is an agent rather than a person, the same rules matter more: typed, documented commands that return structured results can be called and parsed reliably, while free-text reports must be scraped and break when wording changes.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD documentation on its Tcl and Python interfaces; the SWIG documentation; John Ousterhout, "Scripting: Higher-Level Programming for the 21st Century", IEEE Computer, 1998.

problems.q:
Besides Tcl, what scripting interface does OpenROAD offer for working with its database and engines?

A) No other interface; Tcl is the only way in

B) A Python interface to the same engines and database objects

C) A Perl interface only for reports

D) A JavaScript interface running in a browser
problems.a: A Python interface to the same engines and database objects
problems.e: OpenROAD can run with a Python interpreter, giving access to the database objects and engine calls, which suits data analysis and machine-learning work.

problems.q:
Why have EDA tools kept Tcl as their command language for decades?

A) It is small, embeddable and SDC is already written in it

B) It is the fastest language for numerical kernels

C) It has the strictest type system

D) Foundries require it for signoff
problems.a: It is small, embeddable and SDC is already written in it
problems.e: Tcl is easy to embed in a C or C++ application, and SDC, the constraint language, is Tcl. Speed comes from the compiled engines, not from Tcl.

problems.q:
How are C++ database classes usually made callable from Tcl and Python in open EDA tools?

A) A wrapper generator produces bindings from the C++ headers or interface files

B) Each class is rewritten by hand in both languages

C) The C++ code is compiled to Tcl bytecode

D) The scripts parse the C++ source at run time
problems.a: A wrapper generator produces bindings from the C++ headers or interface files
problems.e: Tools such as SWIG generate glue code that maps C++ classes and methods to script objects, so one C++ API serves several languages.

problems.q:
Which task needs a compiled C++ extension rather than a script?

A) Selecting which corner to analyze

B) Printing a summary of utilization

C) Reading a configuration file of 20 parameters

D) A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times
problems.a: A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times
problems.e: Inner-loop work runs millions of times and must be compiled. Scripts orchestrate and configure; they should not sit in hot loops.

problems.q:
Which task needs a compiled C++ extension rather than a script?

A) Reading a configuration file of 20 parameters

B) Selecting which corner to analyze

C) A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times

D) Printing a summary of utilization
problems.a: A new detailed-placement move evaluated millions of times
problems.e: Inner-loop work runs millions of times and must be compiled. Scripts orchestrate and configure; they should not sit in hot loops.

problems.q:
A script loops over all 2 million instances in Python, calling one database getter per instance for its location, and it takes minutes. What is the usual fix?

A) Save the design to DEF first

B) Add more threads to the Python loop

C) Move the loop into a compiled command or fetch data in bulk

D) Rewrite the same loop in Tcl
problems.a: Move the loop into a compiled command or fetch data in bulk
problems.e: Each script-to-C++ call has overhead far above the work of one getter. Bulk calls or a compiled command amortize the crossing.

problems.q:
A Tcl command returns a list of 100,000 object names as one string, and the script then looks each name up again. What design would avoid the waste?

A) Return a longer string

B) Write the names to a file

C) Return object handles or a collection that commands accept directly

D) Require the user to type the names
problems.a: Return object handles or a collection that commands accept directly
problems.e: Name round-trips cost string building and hashing. Collections of handles, as in SDC-style get commands, pass objects without re-lookup.

problems.q:
A Python script calls an engine, which throws a C++ exception. What should the binding layer do?

A) Translate it into a Python exception with the message

B) Ignore it and return zero

C) Let the process abort

D) Print it and continue with stale data
problems.a: Translate it into a Python exception with the message
problems.e: Exceptions must not cross the language boundary raw. The binding catches them and raises a script-level error that the caller can handle.

problems.q:
A tool exposes a Python API and an agent will drive it. Which property of the API matters most for the agent?

A) Commands that print human-only text

B) Typed, documented calls that return structured results

C) As many commands as possible

D) Short command names
problems.a: Typed, documented calls that return structured results
problems.e: An agent needs to know argument types and to parse the result. Free-text output must be scraped and breaks when wording changes.

label: Domain-specific languages for EDA
lesson:
# Domain-specific languages for EDA

EDA is full of small languages: SDC for constraints, Liberty for cell libraries, UPF for power intent, rule decks for DRC and LVS, synthesis scripts, and flow configuration files. A tool designer must decide, for each new kind of input, whether it is an embedded language hosted in Tcl or Python, or an external declarative format with its own parser, and how it will be validated. Those choices decide what users can express and what tools can analyze.

## Embedded and external DSLs

An embedded DSL adds domain commands to a host language. SDC is the classic case: create_clock and set_input_delay are commands run by a Tcl interpreter inside the timer, so SDC inherits Tcl variables, loops and procedures. UPF and many flow scripts follow the same pattern. An external DSL has its own grammar and parser. Liberty is one: groups and attributes describing cells, with no variables or loops. Declarative configuration in YAML or JSON is another. Embedding is cheap to build and powerful to use, because the host language provides parsing, expressions and control flow for free. External declarative formats are easier to analyze: a tool can validate them against a schema, compare two versions, or generate them from a program without running any code. Yosys scripts sit between, as a command language that names passes in a registry and orders them.

## Validation and semantic checks

A DSL is only as good as its error reporting. Syntax errors are found by the parser, but most real mistakes are semantic: a clock with a negative period, a delay on a port that does not exist, a misspelled configuration key. Semantic checks belong where the context is known, when the command executes or the key is read, and they should name the file and line. Silent defaults are the worst failure: a flow configuration with PLACE_DENSTY misspelled that quietly uses the default density produces wrong results with no error. Declaring a schema, the known keys with their types and ranges, and rejecting unknown keys turns such typos into immediate failures. The same discipline makes a DSL safe to accept from automated sources: an agent proposing flow parameters through a validated schema can only touch the intended knobs.

## Analyzing and trusting DSL programs

The power of an embedded DSL limits what can be known without running it. An SDC file that uses a Tcl loop to generate 10,000 false-path commands has those commands only after evaluation, so a static checker must execute the Tcl, or a restricted subset of it, to see them. A declarative rule language, by contrast, exposes its structure, letting an engine reorder rules, share work among them and run them in parallel. Trust is the other issue. A full Tcl interpreter can execute shell commands, open files and sockets; when input may come from an agent or another team, the tool needs a safe interpreter or a restricted command set. Finally, the meaning of a configuration key can change between tool versions. Versioning the schema and recording it with every run lets a regression explain why the same input gave different results.

## Going deeper

Martin Fowler, "Domain-Specific Languages" (2010); the Synopsys Design Constraints format documentation; the Liberty reference manual's description of its syntax.

problems.q:
SDC constraints are commands executed by a Tcl interpreter inside the tool. What kind of domain-specific language is SDC?

A) An embedded DSL hosted in Tcl

B) A binary format

C) A markup language like XML

D) A standalone compiled language
problems.a: An embedded DSL hosted in Tcl
problems.e: SDC adds domain commands such as create_clock to Tcl and inherits Tcl syntax, variables and control flow.

problems.q:
What is the main advantage of a declarative external DSL such as a YAML or JSON flow configuration?

A) A tool can validate and diff it without executing anything

B) It can express any computation

C) It runs faster than compiled code

D) It removes the need for a schema
problems.a: A tool can validate and diff it without executing anything
problems.e: Declarative data can be checked against a schema, compared between runs and generated by programs safely.

problems.q:
What is the main advantage of an embedded DSL over an external one for tool configuration?

A) It is always faster to execute

B) It cannot have syntax errors

C) It needs no documentation

D) It reuses the host language's parser, variables and control flow
problems.a: It reuses the host language's parser, variables and control flow
problems.e: Embedding gives loops, procedures and expressions for free. The cost is that users can write arbitrary code, which is harder to analyze.

problems.q:
A user writes create_clock with a period of -2 in an SDC file. When should a well-designed reader report it?

A) Never; negative periods are legal

B) Only at tape-out

C) Only after timing analysis finishes

D) When the command executes, with the file and line
problems.a: When the command executes, with the file and line
problems.e: Semantic checks belong at the command, where the context is known, so the user can fix the source line.

problems.q:
A flow config has the key PLACE_DENSTY (misspelled). The flow silently uses the default density. What DSL design choice would catch it?

A) Reject unknown keys against a declared schema

B) Make all keys optional

C) Accept any key for flexibility

D) Store config in environment variables
problems.a: Reject unknown keys against a declared schema
problems.e: Silently ignoring unknown keys turns typos into wrong results. A schema with known keys and types fails fast.

problems.q:
A user writes create_clock with a period of -2 in an SDC file. When should a well-designed reader report it?

A) Never; negative periods are legal

B) When the command executes, with the file and line

C) Only after timing analysis finishes

D) Only at tape-out
problems.a: When the command executes, with the file and line
problems.e: Semantic checks belong at the command, where the context is known, so the user can fix the source line.

problems.q:
A DSL for design rules lets authors write each rule as a declarative expression. What does that let the engine do that imperative scripts would not?

A) Avoid storing geometry

B) Run without a layout

C) Analyze, reorder and batch rules for efficient evaluation

D) Skip checking rules
problems.a: Analyze, reorder and batch rules for efficient evaluation
problems.e: Declarative rules expose their structure, so the engine can share work across rules and run them in parallel.

problems.q:
Two versions of a tool interpret the same configuration key differently. What practice prevents silent changes in results?

A) Never change the tool

B) Version the schema and record it with every run

C) Remove the key

D) Let each user decide
problems.a: Version the schema and record it with every run
problems.e: A versioned schema makes changes explicit, and recording it with results lets a regression explain a difference.

problems.q:
A DSL for design rules lets authors write each rule as a declarative expression. What does that let the engine do that imperative scripts would not?

A) Avoid storing geometry

B) Run without a layout

C) Skip checking rules

D) Analyze, reorder and batch rules for efficient evaluation
problems.a: Analyze, reorder and batch rules for efficient evaluation
problems.e: Declarative rules expose their structure, so the engine can share work across rules and run them in parallel.

label: Parsing structural Verilog netlists
prereqs: Netlists as the shared currency of the flow
lesson:
# Parsing structural Verilog netlists

After synthesis, a design travels as a structural Verilog netlist: a module with ports, wire declarations and instances of library cells. Every back-end tool starts by parsing this text into its object model, turning ports into block terminals, instances into instance objects, and each connection into an instance terminal on a net. A tool designer must know exactly what the text implies, because a mis-parsed connection silently becomes a wrong circuit.

## Instances, nets and terminals in the text

Read `module top (a, b, y0); input a, b; output y0; wire n1; NAND2_X1 u1 (.A1(a), .A2(b), .ZN(n1)); INV_X1 u2 (.A(n1), .ZN(y0)); endmodule`. The parser creates two instances, u1 and u2. Each port becomes a block terminal (BTerm) and also names a net, so the nets are a, b, y0 and the wire n1: four nets. Each instance pin becomes an instance terminal (ITerm): u1 has three pins and u2 two, so five ITerms. A useful invariant for a netlist where every cell has one output: each instance drives exactly one net, so the net count is the number of primary inputs plus the number of instances. If the count from the parser disagrees, something was dropped or duplicated.

## Fanout from named connections

A named connection `.A2(n1)` binds pin A2 of the instance to net n1, whatever order the connections are written in. The parser looks up A2 on the cell master, finds its direction from the library, and attaches an ITerm to n1. The fanout of a net is the number of input pins it drives. In `NAND2_X1 u3 (.A1(n1), .A2(n1), .ZN(n2)); INV_X1 u4 (.A(n1), .ZN(y0));`, net n1 drives u3/A1, u3/A2 and u4/A: fanout 3, even though only two instances read it, because each pin is a separate sink. Output pins such as ZN are drivers and are not counted. Fanout feeds everything downstream: load capacitance for timing, net weights for placement, and buffering decisions.

## Positional connections need the cell's port order

Verilog also allows positional connections: `NAND2_X1 u5 (n1, b, n3);` binds signals to ports in the order the cell's module declares them. The netlist alone cannot tell you which signal is the output: the parser needs the port order, from a Verilog cell library or from the order the tool assumes for the master. If NAND2_X1 is declared as (A1, A2, ZN), then n1 is A1, b is A2 and n3 is the output ZN. Get the order wrong and the parser silently turns an output into an input, creating a net with two drivers and a dangling sink. Robust readers therefore check that every net has exactly one driver after reading, and treat positional connections to cells without a declared port order as an error. Escaped identifiers such as `\bus[3] ` (a backslash name ended by whitespace) are another trap for hand-written lexers.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1364-2005, the Verilog standard, sections on module instantiation; the Yosys manual on reading and writing netlists; the OpenROAD documentation for read_verilog and link_design.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, y0, y1, y2); input a, b; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1, n2; NOR2_X1 u1 (.A1(b), .A2(a), .ZN(n1)); NAND2_X1 u2 (.A1(a), .A2(n1), .ZN(y0)); AND2_X1 u3 (.A1(a), .A2(b), .ZN(n2)); AOI21_X1 u4 (.A(b), .B1(n2), .B2(b), .ZN(y1)); BUF_X1 u5 (.A(n2), .Z(y2)); endmodule` How many nets does the block contain? Count every distinct signal, ports included.
problems.e: Each port is also a net: 2 inputs and 3 outputs, plus 2 declared wires, gives 7 nets. Every instance drives exactly one net here, so the count is inputs plus instances.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, y0, y1); input a, b; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2, n3, n4; NAND3_X1 u1 (.A1(a), .A2(a), .A3(a), .ZN(n1)); BUF_X1 u2 (.A(n1), .Z(n2)); AOI21_X1 u3 (.A(b), .B1(n1), .B2(a), .ZN(n3)); NAND3_X1 u4 (.A1(n2), .A2(n1), .A3(n3), .ZN(n4)); AND2_X1 u5 (.A1(n4), .A2(n3), .ZN(y0)); BUF_X1 u6 (.A(n2), .Z(y1)); endmodule` How many nets does the block contain? Count every distinct signal, ports included.
problems.e: Each port is also a net: 2 inputs and 2 outputs, plus 4 declared wires, gives 8 nets. Every instance drives exactly one net here, so the count is inputs plus instances.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, c, d, y0, y1); input a, b, c, d; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2, n3; NOR2_X1 u1 (.A1(c), .A2(a), .ZN(n1)); INV_X1 u2 (.A(b), .ZN(n2)); AND2_X1 u3 (.A1(d), .A2(n1), .ZN(n3)); AOI21_X1 u4 (.A(n2), .B1(n3), .B2(d), .ZN(y0)); AND2_X1 u5 (.A1(n3), .A2(b), .ZN(y1)); endmodule` How many nets does the block contain? Count every distinct signal, ports included.
problems.e: Each port is also a net: 4 inputs and 2 outputs, plus 3 declared wires, gives 9 nets. Every instance drives exactly one net here, so the count is inputs plus instances.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1, y2); input a, b, c; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1, n2; INV_X1 u1 (.A(b), .ZN(n1)); NAND3_X1 u2 (.A1(n1), .A2(n1), .A3(n1), .ZN(n2)); NAND2_X1 u3 (.A1(a), .A2(c), .ZN(y0)); BUF_X1 u4 (.A(n2), .Z(y1)); AND2_X1 u5 (.A1(n2), .A2(n1), .ZN(y2)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net n1 drive (its fanout)?
problems.e: Scan every connection for n1 and keep the input pins: u2/A1, u2/A2, u2/A3 and u5/A2, which is 4.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist: `module top (a, b, y0, y1, y2); input a, b; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1, n2; INV_X1 u1 (.A(b), .ZN(n1)); INV_X1 u2 (.A(n1), .ZN(y0)); AND2_X1 u3 (.A1(b), .A2(n1), .ZN(n2)); INV_X1 u4 (.A(b), .ZN(y1)); BUF_X1 u5 (.A(n2), .Z(y2)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net b drive (its fanout)?
problems.e: Scan every connection for b and keep the input pins: u1/A, u3/A1 and u4/A, which is 3.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist: `module top (a, b, c, d, y0, y1, y2); input a, b, c, d; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1, n2; INV_X1 u1 (.A(a), .ZN(n1)); NAND3_X1 u2 (.A1(c), .A2(b), .A3(n1), .ZN(n2)); NAND2_X1 u3 (.A1(c), .A2(n1), .ZN(y0)); INV_X1 u4 (.A(n1), .ZN(y1)); NAND3_X1 u5 (.A1(n2), .A2(n1), .A3(n2), .ZN(y2)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net n1 drive (its fanout)?
problems.e: Scan every connection for n1 and keep the input pins: u2/A3, u3/A2, u4/A and u5/A2, which is 4.

problems.q: Some instances below connect by position. The library declares the port orders AND2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); INV_X1 (A, ZN); NAND2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN). Netlist: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1); input a, b, c; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2; AND2_X1 u1 (.A1(b), .A2(b), .ZN(n1)); INV_X1 u2 (.A(c), .ZN(n2)); NAND2_X1 u3 (.A1(n1), .A2(a), .ZN(y0)); INV_X1 u4 (n2, y1); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net b drive?
problems.e: Map each positional connection onto the declared port order, where the last position is the output pin. The input pins on b are u1/A1 and u1/A2, which is 2.

problems.q: Some instances below connect by position. The library declares the port orders NAND2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); AOI21_X1 (A, B1, B2, ZN); NAND3_X1 (A1, A2, A3, ZN); INV_X1 (A, ZN). Netlist: `module top (a, b, y0, y1); input a, b; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2; NAND2_X1 u1 (.A1(a), .A2(a), .ZN(n1)); AOI21_X1 u2 (.A(n1), .B1(a), .B2(a), .ZN(n2)); NAND3_X1 u3 (n2, n1, n1, y0); INV_X1 u4 (.A(n1), .ZN(y1)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net a drive?
problems.e: Map each positional connection onto the declared port order, where the last position is the output pin. The input pins on a are u1/A1, u1/A2, u2/B1 and u2/B2, which is 4.

problems.q: Some instances below connect by position. The library declares the port orders AND2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); INV_X1 (A, ZN); AOI21_X1 (A, B1, B2, ZN); NAND3_X1 (A1, A2, A3, ZN); NOR2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN). Netlist: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1, y2); input a, b, c; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1, n2, n3, n4; AND2_X1 u1 (a, b, n1); INV_X1 u2 (.A(b), .ZN(y0)); AOI21_X1 u3 (.A(n1), .B1(n1), .B2(c), .ZN(n2)); INV_X1 u4 (.A(a), .ZN(n3)); NAND3_X1 u5 (n2, n1, c, n4); NOR2_X1 u6 (n4, n3, y1); INV_X1 u7 (n2, y2); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net n1 drive?
problems.e: Map each positional connection onto the declared port order, where the last position is the output pin. The input pins on n1 are u3/A, u3/B1 and u5/A2, which is 3.

label: Parsing Liberty
lesson:
# Parsing Liberty

Liberty (.lib) files carry the timing, power and function of every library cell, and every synthesis, timing and power tool must read them. The format is a simple nested grammar of groups and attributes, but real libraries are huge and full of vendor extensions. A tool designer must parse the grammar generically, interpret the timing semantics correctly, and do both fast enough for files of hundreds of megabytes.

## Groups, simple and complex attributes

Liberty has three statement shapes. A group has a name, a parenthesized argument and a braced body: `cell (NAND2_X1) { ... }`, `pin (A1) { ... }`, `timing () { ... }`. A simple attribute is `name : value ;`, for example `direction : input ;` or `time_unit : "1ns" ;`. A complex attribute is `name (v1, v2, ...) ;`, for example `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` or `index_1 ("0.01, 0.04, 0.16") ;`. Because every statement has one of these three shapes whatever its name, one small recursive-descent parser can build a generic tree of groups and attributes for any Liberty file, including vendor attributes it has never seen. A second pass interprets the tree into cells, pins and arcs. This split keeps the grammar code tiny and puts all the semantics in one place.

## What the parser must keep for timing

Timing lives in `timing ()` groups inside the pin where the arc ends. For the arc from A1 to ZN of a NAND2, the group sits inside `pin (ZN)` with `related_pin : "A1"` and `timing_sense : negative_unate`. Inside it, tables such as `cell_rise (delay_template_7x7)` and `rise_transition (...)` hold `index_1`, `index_2` and `values`. The template name points to an `lu_table_template` declared earlier at library level, whose `variable_1` and `variable_2` say which axis is input transition and which is output load. The parser must keep the template binding, both index vectors, the value matrix (checking it has as many rows as index_1 entries and columns as index_2 entries), the related pin, the timing sense and any `when` condition. The output pin's `function` string, such as `"!(A1 & A2)"`, gives the logic that synthesis needs.

## Scale, streaming and the header

A library for one process corner can run to hundreds of megabytes, almost all of it tables. A placer needs only areas and pin capacitances; a timer needs the tables but maybe not the power data. A streaming parser that interprets the groups it needs and skips the rest, while still tracking brace nesting, saves both time and memory. Order matters: units such as `time_unit` and `capacitive_load_unit` and the table templates are declared in the library header before the cells, so a parser can convert values as it reads them. A table that names an undeclared template is an error, not something to guess at. Several libraries in one session can use different units, so conversion into the tool's internal units must happen per library at read time. Error messages need file and line numbers, since users fix libraries by hand.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual (the open Liberty specification); the OpenSTA source for its Liberty reader; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter on cell libraries.

problems.q:
A Liberty parser meets `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` in the library header. Which construct is it?

A) A complex attribute: a name with a parenthesized value list

B) A group: a name, arguments and a braced body

C) A simple attribute: a name, a colon and one value

D) A define statement that declares a new attribute
problems.a: A complex attribute: a name with a parenthesized value list
problems.e: Liberty has three statement shapes. Simple attributes use `name : value ;`, complex attributes use `name (v1, v2, ...) ;`, and groups add a braced body.

problems.q:
Why can one grammar parse every Liberty file even though vendors add their own attributes?

A) The grammar lists every legal attribute name explicitly

B) Unknown attributes are rejected, so files only use standard names

C) Vendors must register each attribute with the parser at build time

D) Every statement is a group, a simple attribute or a complex attribute, whatever its name
problems.a: Every statement is a group, a simple attribute or a complex attribute, whatever its name
problems.e: The syntax does not depend on the attribute vocabulary. A parser can keep or skip unknown names and still recover the structure.

problems.q:
Which statement is a Liberty group rather than an attribute?

A) `index_1 ("0.01, 0.04, 0.16") ;`

B) `time_unit : "1ns" ;`

C) `direction : input ;`

D) `pin (A1) { direction : input ; capacitance : 0.0016 ; }`
problems.a: `pin (A1) { direction : input ; capacitance : 0.0016 ; }`
problems.e: A group has a name, an argument list and a braced body holding further statements; the others are simple or complex attributes.

problems.q:
A `cell_rise (delay_template_7x7)` group has index_1, index_2 and values. What must the parser resolve to interpret the indices?

A) The lu_table_template named delay_template_7x7, which says which variable each index is

B) The default_max_transition of the library

C) The related_pin of the next timing group

D) The cell's area attribute
problems.a: The lu_table_template named delay_template_7x7, which says which variable each index is
problems.e: The template declares variable_1 and variable_2, for example input transition and output load, so the parser knows which axis is which and can fall back to its default indices.

problems.q:
In a Liberty cell, where does the timing group for the arc from input A1 to output ZN live?

A) Directly under the cell, outside any pin

B) Inside pin (A1), with `related_pin : "ZN"`

C) In the library header, keyed by cell name

D) Inside pin (ZN), with `related_pin : "A1"`
problems.a: Inside pin (ZN), with `related_pin : "A1"`
problems.e: Timing groups sit in the pin they arrive at, and related_pin names the pin the arc starts from.

problems.q:
The values attribute of a 7 × 7 table arrives as seven quoted strings of comma-separated numbers. What must the parser check before storing it?

A) That the values increase along both axes

B) That it has as many rows as index_1 entries and as many columns as index_2 entries

C) That index_1 and index_2 have equal values

D) That every value is positive
problems.a: That it has as many rows as index_1 entries and as many columns as index_2 entries
problems.e: The shape is fixed by the indices; a mismatch is a malformed table. Monotonicity and sign are not required, since negative delays can appear in some tables.

problems.q:
A user complains that a cell's timing in the tool differs from the vendor's datasheet. The parser kept only the first timing group per pin. What was lost?

A) The cell area and leakage power

B) The arcs from other related pins, and conditional (when) arcs for the same pin

C) The library's time unit

D) The pin's direction attribute
problems.a: The arcs from other related pins, and conditional (when) arcs for the same pin
problems.e: An output pin carries one timing group per related pin and often several state-dependent groups. Keeping one drops real arcs.

problems.q:
A library for one corner is several hundred megabytes, but a placer needs only pin capacitances and cell areas. What parser design fits best?

A) A streaming parser that interprets the groups it needs and skips the bodies it does not

B) A full in-memory tree of every group, then a query pass

C) Converting the file to XML first, then parsing the XML

D) Reading only the first megabyte, where the cells are
problems.a: A streaming parser that interprets the groups it needs and skips the bodies it does not
problems.e: Most of the bytes are timing and power tables. Skipping unneeded groups while still tracking brace nesting saves time and memory.

problems.q:
A parser reads `cell_rise (tmpl_A)` before it has seen any lu_table_template named tmpl_A. What should it do?

A) Search the next library file for the template

B) Silently treat the table as scalar

C) Assume a 7 × 7 template with default indices

D) Report an error, because templates must be declared before tables refer to them
problems.a: Report an error, because templates must be declared before tables refer to them
problems.e: Templates are declared at library level before use. Guessing a template would misread the axes and corrupt every delay looked up from that table.

label: Liberty units and scaling
lesson:
# Liberty units and scaling

Liberty tables are just numbers; their meaning comes from unit attributes in the library header. A delay of 0.05 is 50 ps in one library and 0.05 ps in another. Every reader must scale each value by its library's units into one internal unit system, and every consumer must trust that it did. Unit bugs are silent: the tool runs, and every slack is wrong by a factor of a thousand.

## Time units scale delay tables

The header attribute `time_unit` takes one of the values "1ps", "10ps", "100ps" or "1ns", and every delay and transition value in the library is a multiple of it. With `time_unit : "1ns" ;`, a `cell_rise` entry of 0.0532 is $0.0532 \times 1000 = 53.2$ ps. With "10ps", an entry of 5.32 is also 53.2 ps. The input-transition axis of a table (index_1 in a typical delay template) is in the same time unit. A reader converts at parse time: it computes the factor once from the header, multiplies each value as it stores it, and keeps everything internally in one unit, often seconds as a double, so that engines never see library units at all.

## Capacitive load units scale pins and indices

Capacitance uses the complex attribute `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` or `(1,ff)`. Pin capacitances and the output-load axis of delay tables (often index_2) are multiples of it. A pin with `capacitance : 0.0016 ;` in a pF library is 1.6 fF. The conversion runs both ways. When a timer computes a net load of 4.5 fF and must look it up in a pF table, it needs the index value $4.5 / 1000 = 0.0045$. Doing the lookup with 4.5 instead would land far beyond the table's last index and extrapolate wildly. Libraries also declare `voltage_unit`, `current_unit`, `pulling_resistance_unit` and `leakage_power_unit`, each handled the same way.

## Units belong to each library

A session often loads several libraries: standard cells, IO cells, memories from a generator. Nothing forces them to share units. Suppose library A uses "1ns" and library B uses "1ps", and a path has arc delays 0.12 (A), 35 (B) and 0.08 (A). The path delay is $120 + 35 + 80 = 235$ ps. Adding the raw numbers gives 35.2, which means nothing. This is why scaling belongs in the reader, per library, rather than in the timer: the timer adds delays from many cells and cannot know which library each number came from unless the reader already normalized it. A related trap is SDC: its numbers are unitless and take their meaning from `set_units` or from the library units, so changing libraries can silently change what a constraint means.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual, library-level attributes; the OpenSTA source for unit handling in its Liberty reader.

problems.q: A Liberty library header declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;`. A cell_fall table entry for one arc reads 0.1787. What is that delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Table values are in the library time unit, 1ns = 1000 ps, so 0.1787 × 1000 = 178.7 ps.

problems.q: A Liberty library header declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;`. A cell_fall table entry for one arc reads 0.1235. What is that delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Table values are in the library time unit, 1ns = 1000 ps, so 0.1235 × 1000 = 123.5 ps.

problems.q: A Liberty library header declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;`. A rise_transition table entry for one arc reads 0.0894. What is that delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Table values are in the library time unit, 1ns = 1000 ps, so 0.0894 × 1000 = 89.4 ps.

problems.q: A Liberty library declares `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` and an input pin has `capacitance : 0.0084 ;`. What is the pin capacitance in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Capacitance values are in the load unit (1,pf), which is 1000 fF, so the pin is 8.4 fF.

problems.q: A timer must look up an output load of 18.7 fF in a delay table whose index_2 is total_output_net_capacitance. The library declares `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;`. What index_2 value, in library units, corresponds to that load? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: Index values share the load unit, 1000 fF per unit, so 18.7 fF is 0.0187 library units.

problems.q: A Liberty library declares `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` and an input pin has `capacitance : 0.0063 ;`. What is the pin capacitance in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Capacitance values are in the load unit (1,pf), which is 1000 fF, so the pin is 6.3 fF.

problems.q: A path crosses cells from two libraries. Library A declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;` and library B declares `time_unit : "1ps" ;`. The arc delays read from the tables are 0.086 from library A, 271 from library B, 0.059 from library A, 125 from library B. What is the path delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each value is scaled by its own library's unit before summing: A values × 1000, B values × 1, for 541 ps. Adding the raw numbers (396.145) mixes units.

problems.q: A path crosses cells from two libraries. Library A declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;` and library B declares `time_unit : "10ps" ;`. The arc delays read from the tables are 0.021 from library A, 20.7 from library B, 0.189 from library A, 8.1 from library B. What is the path delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each value is scaled by its own library's unit before summing: A values × 1000, B values × 10, for 498 ps. Adding the raw numbers (29.01) mixes units.

problems.q: A path crosses cells from two libraries. Library A declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;` and library B declares `time_unit : "100ps" ;`. The arc delays read from the tables are 0.183 from library A, 0.36 from library B, 0.16 from library A, 0.34 from library B, 0.264 from library A. What is the path delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each value is scaled by its own library's unit before summing: A values × 1000, B values × 100, for 677 ps. Adding the raw numbers (1.307) mixes units.

label: Parsing LEF and DEF
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# Parsing LEF and DEF

LEF and DEF are the physical interchange formats of digital implementation. LEF describes the technology and the abstract of each cell; DEF describes one design's floorplan, instances, pins, nets and routing. A design database such as OpenDB follows their structure closely, so reading them is how a physical tool comes to life. A reader must map each section onto database objects and resolve every cross-reference between the two files.

## Technology LEF and cell LEF

LEF comes in two parts. Technology LEF defines units (`DATABASE MICRONS`), the manufacturing grid, routing and cut layers (with DIRECTION, PITCH, WIDTH and SPACING), via definitions and placement SITEs. Cell LEF defines one MACRO per library cell: its CLASS (CORE, PAD, BLOCK...), its SIZE w BY h in microns, the SITE it fits, and its PINs with DIRECTION, USE and PORT shapes on layers. OBS lists internal metal that routes must avoid. LEF is deliberately an abstract: it gives a router the pin access shapes and blockages but not the transistors inside, and it holds no timing. Pin capacitance and delay come from Liberty, which is why a timer needs both files.

## DEF sections and what they build

A DEF begins with VERSION, DESIGN and `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS n`, then DIEAREA. ROW statements create the placement rows from the LEF site, TRACKS the legal routing tracks per layer and GCELLGRID the global-routing tiles. COMPONENTS creates instances: `- u7 NAND2_X1 + PLACED ( 3800 5600 ) FS ;` gives the master, a status (PLACED, FIXED, UNPLACED) and an orientation (N, S, FN, FS and so on). PINS creates the block's ports with their shapes. NETS gives connectivity as lists of (instance pin) pairs, plus routing once routed; SPECIALNETS carries power straps and rings; BLOCKAGES carries placement and routing blockages. Each section maps onto a database object kind, which is why a DEF reader is a sequence of section handlers.

## Reading order and cross-references

DEF refers to LEF by name: components name masters, ROWs name sites, routing names layers and vias. So LEF must be read first, and every name must resolve. When a NETS entry says `( u7 A3 )` but the master has only A1, A2 and ZN, the reader should report the error with a line number and keep going, never invent a pin. Units must also agree: the DEF resolution may not be finer than the LEF `DATABASE MICRONS`, so a 2000 LEF with a 1000 DEF is fine. Scale matters too. A large DEF can be tens of gigabytes, mostly NETS. The Si2 reference parsers, which OpenDB builds on, are callback-driven: the parser hands each component or net to the database as it is read, instead of building an intermediate tree.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference (distributed with the Si2 LEF/DEF parsers); the OpenDB documentation in OpenROAD; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1.

problems.q:
A PIN in a cell LEF has a PORT with RECT shapes on metal1. What does a parser store for it?

A) The pin's logic function

B) The pin's capacitance for timing

C) The pin's placement in the die

D) The pin's access geometry, which the router uses to connect wires to the pin
problems.a: The pin's access geometry, which the router uses to connect wires to the pin
problems.e: LEF describes physical abstraction: shapes and layers. Electrical data such as capacitance comes from Liberty.

problems.q:
A reader finds LAYER metal2 with DIRECTION, PITCH, WIDTH and SPACING statements. Which file is it reading?

A) A technology LEF

B) A Liberty library

C) The DEF NETS section

D) A cell LEF
problems.a: A technology LEF
problems.e: Technology LEF defines the routing layers, vias, sites and units; cell LEF defines MACROs.

problems.q:
Which LEF content does a placer need to put a standard cell into a row?

A) The MACRO's SIZE, its SITE and its CLASS

B) The VIA definitions

C) The MACRO's PIN shapes on metal1 only

D) The routing layer PITCH values
problems.a: The MACRO's SIZE, its SITE and its CLASS
problems.e: SIZE gives the footprint, SITE says which rows it fits, and CLASS separates core cells from pads and blocks.

problems.q:
A DEF has TRACKS and GCELLGRID statements. Which engine relies on them most?

A) The placer, for its site legality

B) The timer, for its clock definitions

C) The router, for its routing grid and its global-routing tiles

D) The parser, for its unit scaling
problems.a: The router, for its routing grid and its global-routing tiles
problems.e: TRACKS define legal wire positions per layer and GCELLGRID the coarse tiles of global routing.

problems.q:
Where does a DEF describe the power and ground straps of the PDN?

A) SPECIALNETS

B) NETS

C) TRACKS

D) BLOCKAGES
problems.a: SPECIALNETS
problems.e: SPECIALNETS carries prerouted special wiring such as power straps and rings; NETS carries regular signal connectivity and routing.

problems.q:
Where does a DEF describe the power and ground straps of the PDN?

A) SPECIALNETS

B) BLOCKAGES

C) NETS

D) TRACKS
problems.a: SPECIALNETS
problems.e: SPECIALNETS carries prerouted special wiring such as power straps and rings; NETS carries regular signal connectivity and routing.

problems.q:
The LEF declares `DATABASE MICRONS 2000` and a DEF says `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000`. Is that consistent?

A) No: the DEF value must be larger

B) No: the two values must be equal

C) Yes: the DEF resolution may not exceed the LEF's, and 1000 is below 2000

D) Yes, but only if both are powers of two
problems.a: Yes: the DEF resolution may not exceed the LEF's, and 1000 is below 2000
problems.e: LEF/DEF require the DEF units to be no finer than the LEF database units, so every DEF integer can be represented exactly.

problems.q:
A DEF NETS entry connects `( u7 A3 )`, but the LEF MACRO for u7's master has only pins A1, A2 and ZN. What should a robust reader do?

A) Create a new pin A3 on the master

B) Drop the whole NETS section

C) Report the unknown pin and keep reading, so the user sees every such error

D) Connect the net to A1 instead
problems.a: Report the unknown pin and keep reading, so the user sees every such error
problems.e: Cross-reference errors are design bugs. Reporting them with line numbers, without inventing pins, is what lets a user fix the input.

problems.q:
Why must a tool read the LEF before the DEF?

A) The DEF NETS section is written inside the LEF

B) DEF components and vias refer to masters, sites and layers that only the LEF defines

C) LEF sets the DEF database units

D) DEF is compressed with a key stored in the LEF
problems.a: DEF components and vias refer to masters, sites and layers that only the LEF defines
problems.e: A DEF component names a master such as NAND2_X1. Without the LEF the reader cannot resolve it, its size or its pins.

label: DEF database units
lesson:
# DEF database units

DEF stores every coordinate as an integer in database units, declared once by `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS n`. Integers make geometry exact and comparisons cheap, but every reader and writer must convert correctly between microns and units, and LEF dimensions arrive in microns. Unit conversion is the first computation any physical-design tool performs, and the source of some of its most confusing bugs.

## From DEF integers to microns

With `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 2000`, one micron is 2000 database units (dbu), so one dbu is 0.5 nm. The component line `- u12 NAND2_X1 + PLACED ( 38000 57600 ) N ;` puts the instance origin at $x = 38000 / 2000 = 19$ um and $y = 57600 / 2000 = 28.8$ um. The value of n is chosen by the writer from a fixed set (100, 200, 1000, 2000 and so on); it must be no finer than the LEF `DATABASE MICRONS`. Inside a database the integers are usually kept as they are, and conversion to microns happens only for reports and user input, so the engines work in exact integer arithmetic. A coordinate that is not a whole number of database units cannot be written at all, which is why a writer that rescales a design to a coarser resolution must snap every shape and report what moved.

## Die area from DIEAREA

`DIEAREA ( 0 0 ) ( 600000 400000 ) ;` with 2000 units per micron is a die of $600000 / 2000 = 300$ um by $400000 / 2000 = 200$ um, so $300 \times 200 = 60000$ square microns. Area scales with the square of the unit: a product of two dbu lengths is in dbu squared, so the conversion divides by $n^2 = 4{,}000{,}000$, not by n. Dividing once is the classic mistake, and gives an area 2000 times too large. When the lower-left corner is not at the origin, as in `DIEAREA ( 2000 2000 ) ( 602000 402000 )`, subtract corners first. DIEAREA can also be a rectilinear polygon with more points, in which case the area comes from the polygon, not the bounding box.

## LEF microns into DEF rows

LEF gives the SITE width in microns, for example 0.19 um. A DEF row `ROW ROW_0 core 3800 5600 N DO 400 BY 1 STEP 380 0 ;` with 2000 units per micron uses a step of $0.19 \times 2000 = 380$ dbu, and its right edge is at $3800 + 400 \times 380 = 155800$ dbu. Every LEF dimension must land on an integer at the DEF resolution, which is one reason resolutions are chosen to match the manufacturing grid: a 0.005 um grid needs at least 200 units per micron. If a conversion produces a fraction, the writer must round, and a rounded site width accumulates error across hundreds of sites in a row, which breaks legality checks in the placer.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference, sections on UNITS, DIEAREA and ROW; the OpenDB documentation on database units.

problems.q: A DEF file declares `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 200 ;` and its COMPONENTS section has `- u4643 INV_X1 + PLACED ( 12598 86970 ) N ;`. What is the x coordinate of the instance origin in microns? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: DEF stores integers in database units; one micron is 200 units, so 12598 / 200 = 62.99 microns.

label: SDC as Tcl
lesson:
# SDC as Tcl

Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) is the language of timing intent: clocks, input and output delays, exceptions. It is not a standalone grammar but a set of Tcl commands, so an SDC file is a Tcl program. A tool that reads SDC must evaluate Tcl and must resolve object queries against its own database. Knowing this explains how constraints work, and how they silently break.

## SDC is a Tcl dialect

Each SDC line is a Tcl command: `create_clock -name clk -period 2.5 [get_ports clk]`. Tcl rules apply. Square brackets are command substitution: `get_ports clk` runs first and its result becomes an argument. A dollar sign before a name substitutes the variable's value, so `set p 2.5` followed by a reference to p after -period is legal. Braces quote literally, so `{in_a in_b}` is one word holding a two-element list. Loops, procedures and expressions are all available: a foreach loop over {a b c} whose body calls set_load on get_ports of the loop variable issues three constraints. A tool that only pattern-matches SDC lines will misread any file that uses these features, which is why real readers embed a Tcl interpreter and define the SDC commands inside it.

## Object queries return collections

Commands such as `get_ports`, `get_pins`, `get_cells`, `get_nets` and `get_clocks` look up database objects by name pattern and return a collection of object handles, not strings. `get_pins u1/*` returns every pin of u1. The constraint command then attaches to those objects. Two consequences follow. A pattern that matches nothing returns an empty collection, and the constraint silently applies to nothing, so careful tools warn on empty matches. And constraints bind through names: if synthesis renames `u_alu/add_0` to `u_alu/add_0_inst`, a constraint written against the old hierarchical name stops matching. Collections exist because re-resolving names for every command would be slow and ambiguous when a port and a net share a name.

## Interpreting SDC inside a tool

SDC numbers are unitless. `set_input_delay 300 -clock clk [get_ports a]` means 300 of whatever time unit is in effect, set by `set_units` or inherited from the library, so a file written for picoseconds and read in nanoseconds is off by a thousand. Tools differ in how much Tcl they allow. OpenSTA defines the SDC commands in its own Tcl interpreter and sources the file. Some sign-off flows use restricted readers that reject arbitrary Tcl, so that a constraint file cannot run side effects and means the same in every tool. Writing SDC back out after optimization is the reverse problem: collections of handles must be turned into names that resolve in the modified netlist.

## Going deeper

The SDC specification published with the open-source SDC parser; the OpenSTA documentation for read_sdc; Gangadharan and Churiwala, "Constraining Designs for Synthesis and Timing Analysis" (2013).

A) Only if the variable is declared with set_units

B) Yes: SDC is Tcl, so variables and substitution work

C) No: square brackets are comments in SDC

D) No: SDC accepts only numeric literals
problems.a: Yes: SDC is Tcl, so variables and substitution work
problems.e: SDC commands are Tcl commands. Variables, expressions, loops and procedures are all available to the file.

problems.a: To reject side effects and tool-specific commands, so the constraints mean the same everywhere
problems.e: A full shell lets a constraint file run arbitrary code. A restricted reader keeps constraints portable and reproducible across tools.

label: Parsing SPEF
lesson:
# Parsing SPEF

SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format) carries the resistances and capacitances extracted from routed wires, net by net. Timers read it to compute wire delays, and it is often the largest file in the flow. A parser must handle the name map that compresses it, the unit header that gives its numbers meaning, and the per-net sections whose RC networks feed delay calculation.

## The name map compresses names

Hierarchical net names are long, and each appears many times in a SPEF: in the *D_NET line, in *CONN entries and in every node name of its RC network. The *NAME_MAP section assigns each name an index such as `*1234`, written once, and the body uses the index. Take the name u_core/u_alu/n_4521 (19 characters) appearing 12 times. Without the map that costs $12 \times 19 = 228$ bytes. With the map, references cost $12 \times 5 = 60$ bytes for the token *1234, and the map line costs $5 + 1 + 19 + 1 = 26$ bytes (index, space, name, newline), so the map saves $228 - 60 - 26 = 142$ bytes. A parser reads the map into a hash table first and resolves every token through it.

## Total capacitance of a D_NET

The header declares units: `*C_UNIT 1 PF`, `*R_UNIT 1 OHM`, `*T_UNIT 1 NS`. Each net section starts `*D_NET n17 <total cap>` followed by *CONN, *CAP and *RES. In *CAP, a line with one node is capacitance to ground, such as `1 n17:1 0.0012`; a line with two nodes is coupling capacitance, such as `3 n17:2 n940:1 0.0004`. The total on the *D_NET line includes both. With entries 0.0012, 0.0008 and coupling 0.0004 in pF, the total is $1.2 + 0.8 + 0.4 = 2.4$ fF. A coupling entry appears in each of the two nets' sections, so it counts toward each net's own total, and a crosstalk-aware timer keeps it as a coupling element rather than grounding it.

## Resistance along a parasitic path

The *RES section lists resistors as (index, node, node, value). Nodes are pins such as u1:ZN or internal points such as n17:3. The network is usually a tree rooted at the driver. With `*R_UNIT 1 KOHM`, the chain u1:ZN to n17:1 (0.012), n17:1 to n17:2 (0.030), n17:2 to u4:A (0.018), plus a branch n17:1 to u7:B (0.025), gives a driver-to-u4:A resistance of $12 + 30 + 18 = 60$ ohms; the branch to u7:B is not on that path. The parser builds an adjacency list over the nodes, then a delay calculator walks it, for example for Elmore delay. Lines can arrive in any order, so a reader must build the graph before walking it, and should flag loops or disconnected nodes.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1481 (the SPEF chapter); the OpenSTA source for its SPEF reader; the OpenRCX documentation in OpenROAD.

problems.q: A SPEF writer can replace the net name u_soc/u_alu/n_54773 (19 characters) by the index *72231 through *NAME_MAP. The name appears 14 times in the file. Each name-map line is the index, a space, the name and a newline. How many bytes does the map save?
problems.e: Without the map the name costs 14 × 19 = 266 bytes. With it, references cost 14 × 6 = 84 and the map line costs 6 + 1 + 19 + 1 = 27, so the saving is 155 bytes.

What is the series resistance from the driver u1:ZN to the sink u4:A, in ohms?

label: GDSII stream records
lesson:
# GDSII stream records

GDSII is the binary stream format in which layouts reach the mask shop, and KLayout, Magic and every DRC engine read and write it. Unlike LEF and DEF it is a flat sequence of typed binary records, so a reader is a loop over record headers. Knowing the record layout lets a tool designer size files, write a minimal reader, and convert stored integers into physical coordinates.

## Record headers and the XY record

Every GDSII record starts with a 4-byte header: a 2-byte big-endian length that counts the whole record including the header, a 1-byte record type (HEADER, BGNLIB, UNITS, BGNSTR, BOUNDARY, XY, ENDEL and so on) and a 1-byte data type (no data, 2-byte integer, 4-byte integer, 8-byte real, ASCII string). A reader reads the header, then length minus 4 bytes of payload, and dispatches on the type. Coordinates live in XY records as pairs of 4-byte signed integers, 8 bytes per point. A BOUNDARY is closed by repeating its first point, so a rectangle with 4 vertices stores 5 points: $4 + 8 \times 5 = 44$ bytes. An L-shaped polygon with 6 vertices stores 7 points, $4 + 56 = 60$ bytes.

## Bytes in a layout element

An element is a sequence of records ending in ENDEL. A BOUNDARY element is BOUNDARY (4 bytes, no data), LAYER (4 + 2), DATATYPE (4 + 2), XY (4 + 8(n + 1)) and ENDEL (4), so an n-vertex boundary costs $24 + 8(n + 1)$ bytes: 64 bytes for a rectangle. A PATH element is a wire with a centerline: PATH, LAYER, DATATYPE, WIDTH (4 + 4, a 4-byte integer), the XY of its k points (not closed, so no repeated point) and ENDEL, which is $28 + 8k$ bytes. A structure holding two rectangles and a 3-point path is $64 + 64 + 52 = 180$ bytes. Sizes like these explain why flat GDS of a large chip runs to many gigabytes, and why hierarchy, with SREF and AREF references to shared structures, and the more compact OASIS format matter.

## Database units to microns

Coordinates are integers in database units. The UNITS record holds two 8-byte reals: the size of a database unit in user units, and its size in meters. A typical library stores 0.001 and 1e-9: one database unit is 1 nm, and the user unit is the micron. An XY integer of 123456 is then $123456 \times 10^{-9}$ m $= 123.456$ um. With a database unit of 5e-10 m the same integer is 61.728 um. A reader must use the meter value, not assume nanometers, and a tool that merges GDS files from different sources, as the final step of a flow merges cell GDS into the design, must rescale any file whose database unit differs, or reject it. The 8-byte reals use the GDSII excess-64 base-16 floating-point format, not IEEE 754, which a hand-written reader must decode explicitly.

## Going deeper

The GDSII Stream Format manual (Calma, release 6.0); the KLayout documentation on stream formats.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a L-shaped polygon with 6 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 6 + 1 = 7 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 7 = 60 bytes.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a polygon with 26 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 26 + 1 = 27 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 27 = 220 bytes.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a U-shaped polygon with 8 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 8 + 1 = 9 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 9 = 76 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A structure holds a 6-vertex boundary. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 80, totalling 80 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A structure holds a 4-vertex boundary, a 4-vertex boundary and a 6-vertex boundary. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 64 + 64 + 80, totalling 208 bytes.

A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A PATH is PATH (4 bytes), LAYER, DATATYPE, WIDTH (header plus a 4-byte integer), XY with its points (an open path does not repeat a point) and ENDEL. A structure holds a 6-vertex boundary, a 4-vertex boundary, a 4-vertex boundary, a 4-vertex boundary and a 3-point PATH with a WIDTH record. How many bytes do these elements occupy?

problems.e: One database unit is 1e-8 m = 0.01 um, so 1467144 units are 14671.44 um.

problems.e: One database unit is 1e-8 m = 0.01 um, so 66660 units are 666.6 um.

problems.e: One database unit is 2.5e-10 m = 0.00025 um, so 408543 units are 102.1358 um.

label: EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF and Si2 standards
prereqs: The map of design representations and formats
lesson:
# EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF and Si2 standards

Beyond Verilog, Liberty, LEF/DEF, SPEF and GDS, a tool meets a set of interchange standards for netlists, IP metadata and power intent. Each comes with its own syntax and its own parsing strategy: S-expressions, XML with a schema, or Tcl. Consortia such as Si2 steward several of them. A tool designer should recognize each format, know what it carries, and know what reader it needs.

## EDIF netlist interchange

EDIF (Electronic Design Interchange Format) describes netlists as nested S-expressions, LISP-style parenthesized lists: libraries contain cells, cells contain views, views have an interface (ports) and contents (instances and nets). One recursive reader can parse any EDIF file, because every construct is a list whose first element is a keyword. The price is verbosity: keywords repeat for every object. EDIF remains common in FPGA flows and older tool hand-offs. The parser's job is the same as for a Verilog netlist: build the same instances, nets and terminals in the object model. Importing the same design from EDIF and from Verilog should give identical connectivity, which is a cheap and powerful regression test for both readers.

## IP-XACT component metadata

IP-XACT (IEEE 1685) is an XML schema for describing IP blocks: components, bus interfaces with their port mappings, memory maps, address blocks and registers with their fields. It does not describe logic. It is the single source from which tools generate register RTL, C header files and documentation, and from which SoC integration tools wire blocks together by matching bus interfaces. A reader uses a standard XML parser and validates against the schema, rather than a hand-written grammar. A register of 32 bits with fields at bit offsets 0, 8 and 16 generates both the decode logic and the software mask constants, so hardware and software cannot drift apart.

## UPF power intent and the Si2 coalitions

UPF (Unified Power Format, IEEE 1801) captures power intent outside the RTL: `create_power_domain`, supply nets and ports, isolation, level shifting, retention and power states. Like SDC it is Tcl, so a tool reads it with a Tcl interpreter that defines these commands, and keeping it separate lets one RTL be implemented under different power strategies. Si2 (Silicon Integration Initiative) is an industry consortium whose member coalitions maintain standards, among them OpenAccess, a design database API, and the reference LEF/DEF parsers on which OpenDB's readers are based. Shared reference parsers matter because a format is only as standard as its corner cases: when tools share a parser, the same file means the same design to each of them.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1685 (IP-XACT); IEEE Std 1801 (UPF); the EDIF 2 0 0 specification; the Si2 OpenAccess documentation.

problems.q:
Why is an S-expression format like EDIF easy to parse but bulky?

A) It requires an XML schema validator

B) It stores coordinates as binary floats

C) It compresses names with a name map

D) Every construct is a parenthesized list, so one recursive reader handles it, but keywords repeat for every object
problems.a: Every construct is a parenthesized list, so one recursive reader handles it, but keywords repeat for every object
problems.e: A uniform list syntax needs one small reader; the price is verbose, keyword-heavy text.

problems.q:
An FPGA vendor tool exports a netlist with nested parenthesized forms such as `(cell ... (view ... (interface ...) (contents ...)))`. Which format is it?

A) IP-XACT

B) UPF

C) SPEF

D) EDIF
problems.a: EDIF
problems.e: EDIF uses LISP-like S-expressions to describe libraries, cells, views, interfaces and contents.

problems.q:
Why is an S-expression format like EDIF easy to parse but bulky?

A) It stores coordinates as binary floats

B) Every construct is a parenthesized list, so one recursive reader handles it, but keywords repeat for every object

C) It compresses names with a name map

D) It requires an XML schema validator
problems.a: Every construct is a parenthesized list, so one recursive reader handles it, but keywords repeat for every object
problems.e: A uniform list syntax needs one small reader; the price is verbose, keyword-heavy text.

problems.q:
An IP vendor ships an XML file describing a block's bus interfaces, memory map and registers. Which standard is it?

A) EDIF

B) UPF (IEEE 1801)

C) Liberty

D) IP-XACT (IEEE 1685)
problems.a: IP-XACT (IEEE 1685)
problems.e: IP-XACT is the XML schema for IP metadata: components, bus interfaces, memory maps and registers.

An IP vendor ships an XML file describing a block's bus interfaces, memory map and registers. Which standard is it?

A) IP-XACT (IEEE 1685)

C) EDIF

D) UPF (IEEE 1801)

problems.e: IP-XACT is the XML schema for IP metadata: components, bus interfaces, memory maps and registers.

An IP vendor ships an XML file describing a block's bus interfaces, memory map and registers. Which standard is it?

problems.e: IP-XACT is the XML schema for IP metadata: components, bus interfaces, memory maps and registers.

OpenDB's LEF and DEF readers trace back to reference parsers distributed through Si2. What does reusing a reference parser buy a tool?

A) Consistent interpretation of the format's corner cases across tools

B) A license to the foundry's PDK

C) Faster placement

D) Automatic timing closure
problems.a: Consistent interpretation of the format's corner cases across tools
problems.e: When several tools use the same reference parser, the files mean the same thing to each of them.

problems.q:
Why is power intent written in UPF rather than in the RTL itself?

A) So the same RTL can be implemented under different power strategies, kept in a separate file

B) Because RTL cannot describe any logic

C) Because power domains are only physical

D) Because UPF replaces the netlist
problems.a: So the same RTL can be implemented under different power strategies, kept in a separate file
problems.e: Separating power intent from function lets verification and implementation share one description without editing the RTL.
